# Introduction
New York City has the largest subway system in the United States, and it serves as an essential part of the city's public infrastructure. There are many benefits to widespread public transportation systems, but maximizing their effectiveness requires an understanding of how people use public transit in their everyday lives.

This exploration and analysis specifically examines New York City's subway ridership in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Queens during the week of September 15-21, 2024. This specific week was chosen because we felt it was likely going to be the best representation of a relatively normal week, meaning there are no holidays, school is in session, and it is not off season.

Specifically, we proposed the following three questions: 
- “How do NYC subway ridership volumes vary throughout the day?”
- "Which hours have the highest ridership average (weekdays vs. weekends)?"
- "Do these hours correspond to commuting periods?"

```{r Read in packages and data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ezids)
library(car)

project <- read.csv("~/Desktop/Cloning-Git/DATS6101-project1/DATS6101_Project_MTA_Subway_Hourly_Ridership.csv")
```

# Data Source and Description

This project uses an hourly NYC subway ridership dataset published by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) during the full seven-day week of September 15–21, 2024 ($N = 553,429$ observations). The dataset was obtained from https://data.ny.gov/Transportation/MTA-Subway-Hourly-Ridership-2020-2024/wujg-7c2s/about_data.

Our area of focus is subway ridership in the four boroughs: Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, and Queens. The data collection method from the MTA is that passenger entries were recorded automatically via turnstile swipes (MetroCard) and contactless taps (OMNY) at 424 station complexes across the boroughs. The data was then cleaned to remove duplication and uses on partner agencies (PATH, etc). Time-late data due to malfunctioning hardware is incorporated as made available.

**Main Variables of Analysis**

These are the following main variables of analysis that we will be using from the original MTA dataset.

| Data Label | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| transit_timestamp | DATE | Rounded down to nearest hour (Swipe at 1:37pm will be reported as 1pm) |
| station_complex_id | ALPHANUMERIC | A unique identifier for station complexes |
| station_complex | TEXT | Subway complex where an entry swipe or tap took place. Large subway complexes have multiple lines |
| borough | TEXT | Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens |
| ridership | NUMERIC | Total number of riders that entered a subway complex |
| transfers | NUMERIC | Number of individuals who entered a subway complex via a free bus-to-subway or free out-of-network transfer. These transfers are included in total ridership. Transfers within a subway complex (e.g., transferring from the 2 to the 4 train within Atlantic Avenue) are not captured here |

# Data Quality and Cleaning

For the data cleaning portion, we first converted all the variables to either numeric or factor. We also checked for any NA values as well as duplicates. There were none for either of these, which ordinarily could have been suspicious, however considering that this data was cleaned by the MTA prior to having been uploaded for public downloads, we interpreted this more as a testament to the MTA's strengths.

```{r Data Cleaning}
# Make sure columns are cast to correct types
project$borough <- as.factor(project$borough)
project$payment_method <- as.factor(project$payment_method)
project$fare_class_category <- as.factor(project$fare_class_category)
project$ridership <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", project$ridership))
project$transfers <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", project$transfers))

# Checking for any NA values
colSums(is.na(project))

# Checking for duplicates 
sum(duplicated(project))

str(project)

# Checking for any negative values to make sure there were no stragglers in the data cleaning 
sum(project$ridership < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(project$transfers < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

```

```{r Data Formatting}
## Created Variables of Analysis
# Add 24-hour time column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp = mdy_hms(transit_timestamp),
    hour = hour(timestamp)
  )

# Add categories for morning, afternoon, evening, night
# Morning (5am - 10:59am), afternoon (11am - 3:59pm), evening (4pm - 8:59pm), night (9pm - 4:59am)
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    time_of_day = case_when(
      hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning",
      hour >= 11 & hour < 16 ~ "Mid Day",
      hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening",
      TRUE ~ "Night"
    )
  )

# Add day of week column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    day_of_week = wday(timestamp, label = TRUE)
  )

# Weekend vs. Weekday column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(day_type = if_else(day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "Weekend", "Weekday"))

# Commuter hours column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    commute_type = case_when(
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning Commute",
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening Commute",
      TRUE ~ "Other Hours"
    )
  )

project$time_of_day <- as.factor(project$time_of_day)
project$day_of_week <- as.factor(project$day_of_week)
project$day_type <- as.factor(project$day_type)
project$commute_type <- as.factor(project$commute_type)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

The EDA had three main analytic goals, to identify patterns across: 

- Time: Which hours/time periods have highest ridership

- Days: Weekday/Weekend comparison, commuting periods

- Geography: Ridership by borough and high bus-to-subway transfers

This dataset contains 553,429 station-hour records across 424 station complexes in the four boroughs. The core numerical metrics evaluated are total ridership (station entries) and transfers (intermodal bus-to-subway entries, which represent a sub-category contained within total ridership). The maximum value of ridership is one to point out reaching 14012 taps, within one hour at one station, with a minimum of 1 a very striking spread.

```{r}

  summarize(hourly_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm=TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%

borough_ridership_means
```

This shows the average number of riders in each borough per timestamp. Includes all stations and times of day. The greatest to least mean total ridership by borough: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, Bronx.

Weekdays (Sept 16-20) display a pronounced bimodal commuting profile, characterized by a sharp morning rush peak at 08:00 AM (~400,000 riders) and an evening peak at 05:00 PM (>420,000 riders). Morning Peak: A steep climb from ~15,000 riders at 03:00 AM to a sharp peak between 300,000 and 420,000 riders at 08:00 AM. Midday Trough: A drop to ~150,000 riders around 11:00 AM–12:00 PM. Evening Peak: A second, even larger surge peaking between 350,000 and 430,000 riders at 05:00 PM (17:00). Late Night: Drops near zero (~10,000-20,000 riders) between 01:00 AM and 04:00 AM. In contrast, weekend curves (Sept 15 & Sept 21) exhibit smooth, flattened arcs peaking gently near ~200,000 riders at 04:00 PM.

The severe dip between rush-hour peaks and midday/overnight hours establishes the definition for commute (Weekday 5:00 AM-10:59 AM and 4:00 PM-8:59 PM). This directly motivated our future Two-Sample t-test.

**Summary Statistics Station Ridership**

```{r Summary-statistics-ridership}
#Station ridership
project %>%
  summarize(
    median = median(ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard_deviation = sd(ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum = min(ridership, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(ridership, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

With the Median of 10 riders/hour and IQR of 27 riders/hour, this means that half of all station-hour observations across the entire MTA network log 10 or fewer passenger entries per hour, so the middle 50% of all station-hour logs fall between 3 and 30 riders. The standard deviation (187.44) is over 18 times larger than the median (10). This massive spread confirms a right-skewed, heavy-tailed distribution. A vast majority of outer-borough neighborhood stations experience not very high entry volumes, while a small handful of massive Manhattan transit hubs handle very high passenger surges during commute hours.

**Summary Statistics Station Transfers**

```{r Summary-statistics-transfers}
#Station transfers
project %>%
  summarize(
    median = median(transfers, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(transfers, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard_deviation = sd(transfers, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum = min(transfers, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(transfers, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

The striking numbers here are that the Median is 0 transfers/hour and as such the IQR is 0 transfers/hour, so at least 75% of all station-hour records in the entire system record exactly 0 bus-to-subway transfers. However, despite a median of zero, the maximum reaches 1,350 transfers in a single hour


Based on the preliminary EDA visual and descriptive metrics, the initial answers to the study's core research questions can be summarized prior to formal hypothesis testing:

1. Temporal Patterns: Subway demand is structured by work-week routines, exhibiting a strong bimodal weekday commute profile that collapses on weekends into a low-volume, unimodal curve.

2. Geographic Distribution: Manhattan functions as the network's volume hub, handling over twice the daily entry volume of any outer borough.

3. Infrastructure Focus: While Manhattan leads in total passenger count, Queens functions as the primary intermodal connection hub.

# Analysis and Interpretation

**Overview**

In order to further analyze the three questions of interest, four different statistical tests were performed on our dataset. These tests consisted of a two-sample t-test comparing mean hourly ridership in commute versus non-commute periods, a two-sample t-test comparing mean hourly ridership between weekdays and weekends, a one-way ANOVA that compares mean hourly ridership between different time-of-day categories (morning, midday, evening, and night), and a one-way ANOVA that compares mean daily ridership between the four boroughs in the dataset.

**Commute vs. Non-Commute t-test**

A two-sample t test was conducted to determine if there was a statistically significant difference between the mean hourly ridership during commute and non-commute periods. Commute periods were classified to be during the morning or evening, which falls between 5:00 AM - 10:59 AM and 4:00 PM - 9:00 PM in the context of this dataset. Non-commute periods were classified as midday and night periods, falling from 11:00 AM - 3:59 PM and 9:00 PM - 4:59 AM. 

The null hypothesis for this test states that the mean hourly ridership during commute periods is equal to the mean hourly ridership during non-commute periods. The alternative hypothesis states that the mean hourly ridership during commute periods is different from the mean hourly ridership during non-commute periods. Before conducting this test, the assumptions were checked. We found that the population standard deviation was unknown given that we took a sample of the data and that the sample size is large enough per the central limit theorem to be robust against a normality violation. The independent observation may be violated due to our data being a time series set, but we continued with the two-sample t-test because it most closely fit the situation we are analyzing.

```{r Commute vs. Non-Commute t-test}
hourly_ridership <- project %>%
  mutate(commute_period = if_else(commute_type %in% c("Morning Commute", "Evening Commute"), "Commute","Non-Commute")) %>%
  group_by(timestamp, day_type, time_of_day, commute_period) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"], col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"], col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)

# t-test for commute time vs. non-commute time means
commute_period_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ commute_period, data = hourly_ridership)
commute_period_test
```

At the $\alpha$ = 0.05 level, this test produced a T statistic equal to 8.7228 with 84.945 degrees of freedom. The associated p-value was 1.975 x 10-13. Given these findings, there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We are able to conclude that there is a statistically significant difference between the mean hourly ridership in the commute periods versus the non-commute periods.

A further look at the t.test output showed that the mean hourly ridership in the commute group was 250,605 riders per hour and the mean hourly ridership between the non-commute group was 104,204.5 riders per hour. Additionally, we are 95% confident that the difference in the mean hourly ridership between the commute and non-commute groups is between 113,029.8 and 179,204.5 riders per hour.

**Weekday vs. Weekend t-test**

A second two-sample t-test was conducted to determine if there was a statistically significant difference between the mean hourly ridership on weekdays versus weekends. For this test, the null hypothesis states that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is equal to the mean hourly ridership on weekends. The alternative hypothesis states that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is different from the mean hourly ridership on weekdays.
	
Before conducting the procedure, the assumptions for the test were analyzed. The population standard deviation is unknown because we took a sample of the whole dataset. We also found that the sample size was large enough for the test to be robust against any violations of normality, which comes from the central limit theorem. Since the data represents a series of time, the independent observation may be violated. However, we decided to proceed once again with this t-test.

```{r Weekday vs. Weekend t-test}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"], col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"], col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)

# t-test for weekday vs. weekend means
weekday_weekend_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ day_type, data = hourly_ridership)
weekday_weekend_test
```

At the $\alpha$ = 0.05 level, the test produced a T statistic of 4.641 with 152.69 degrees of freedom. The associated p-value was 7.411 x 10-6, which allows for the rejection of the null hypothesis. This means that there is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is significantly different than the mean hourly ridership on weekends.
	
When looking at the other associated output from the t-test, we can also see that the mean hourly ridership during weekdays is 171883.8 riders per hour and the mean hourly ridership on weekends is 102756.6 riders per hour. We are also 95% confident that the difference in mean hourly ridership between weekdays and weekends is between 39700.86 and 98553.65 riders per hour.

**ANOVA: Differences in mean hourly ridership between time-of-day categories**

A one way ANOVA test was performed to determine if there were differences between the hourly ridership means during different time-of-day categories. Given our findings from the EDA section, we created four time-of-day categories to put our data in. Observations fell during the morning (5:00 AM - 10:59 AM), mid-day (11:00 AM - 3:59 PM), the evening (4:00 PM - 8:59 PM), or the night (9:00 PM - 4:59 AM).

The null hypothesis for this test states that the mean hourly ridership is equal for the morning, mid-day, evening, and night periods. The alternative hypothesis states that at least one time-of-day category has a different mean hourly ridership from the other categories. 

Before the test was conducted, a check on the ANOVA assumptions was done. Given the assumptions of normality, independence of errors, and homogeneity of variances, there is concern for violation on all three of them. The QQ plots for each time-of-day category show some deviation from the normal distribution, but the sample sizes for each category are large enough for the test to be robust. The output from Levene’s test showed evidence of heteroscedasticity, and our sample was also not selected at random which could violate the independence of errors. These potential violations may be a limitation of this test. Despite these concerns, we decided to continue evaluating with the one way ANOVA test.

```{r Time-of-Day ANOVA}
# Assumptions check
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (time_category in unique(hourly_ridership$time_of_day)) {
  x <- hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$time_of_day == time_category]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", time_category))
  qqline(x, col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)
}

leveneTest(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)

# One way ANOVA test and post hoc
time_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)
summary(time_anova)

time_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(time_anova)
time_post_hoc
```

At the $\alpha$ = 0.05 level, the test produced an F statistic 53.72 with an associated p-value of less than 2 x 10-16. Since the p-value is very small and below the alpha level, there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. This means that we can conclude that there is at least one time-of-day category that has a different mean hourly ridership from the others.

Given that the ANOVA test was statistically significant, we continued onto a post hoc Tukey test that will evaluate the differences between all time-of-day pairings. After running the post hoc analysis, the time period pairings that showed a statistically significant difference were mid-day and evening, morning and evening, night and evening, night and mid-day, and night and morning. Out of these, we found that the differences between mid-day/evening and morning/evening were notable since they include commute periods. We expected the night period to be significantly different from all of the others due to it including the middle of the night.

**ANOVA: Differences in mean daily ridership between boroughs**

A one way ANOVA test was conducted to analyze the differences in mean daily ridership between boroughs. Since our data included the four boroughs of Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Queens, those were the only potential differences that were tested for.

The null hypothesis for this test states that the mean daily ridership in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Queens are all equal to each other. The alternative hypothesis states that at least one borough has a different mean daily ridership than the other boroughs.

Before the test was completed, the assumptions were checked. Given the assumptions of normality, independence of errors, and homogeneity of variances, there is concern for violation on all three of them.  The QQ plots for each borough show deviation from the normal distribution, and the sample sizes for each borough are relatively low. Our sample was also not selected at random. The homogeneity of variances assumption may also be violated, but Levene's test output shows that there is evidence in support of homogeneity of variances at the $\alpha$ = 0.10 level. Given these findings, this may be a limitation of the ANOVA analysis. However, we will continue with running the test to analyze the borough differences.

```{r Borough ANOVA}
# Daily ridership total for each borough
borough_daily <- project %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  group_by(date, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Assumptions check
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (b in unique(borough_daily$borough)) {
  x <- borough_daily$total_ridership[borough_daily$borough == b]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", b))
  qqline(x, col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)
}

leveneTest(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)

# One way ANOVA test: Do daily averages in each borough differ?
borough_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)
summary(borough_anova)

# Post hoc tests
borough_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(borough_anova)
borough_post_hoc
```

At the $\alpha$ = 0.05 level, the test produced an F value of 63.86 with the associated p-value of 1.38 x 10-11. Due to this p-value being smaller than the alpha level, there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. This means that we are able to conclude that at least one borough has a different mean daily ridership than the other boroughs.

Given that the null hypothesis was rejected in the initial ANOVA test, we continued on to conduct a post hoc Tukey test. After running the Tukey test, we found that the borough pairings that had significantly different mean daily ridership values were Brooklyn and the Bronx, Manhattan and the Bronx, Manhattan and Brooklyn, and Queens and Manhattan. From these results, we are able to see that Manhattan’s mean daily ridership differs significantly from all other boroughs.

**Hypothesis Testing of Transfers**

Our primary questions of interest regarding transfers are whether there is a normal distribution of bus-to-subway transfers during 1) commuting periods vs non-commuting periods and 2) during weekdays vs weekends. Additionally, are transfer amounts the same during commuting periods vs non-commuting periods as well as during the week in comparison to the weekend.
  
**T-Tests: Commute vs. Non-commute; Weekday vs. Weekend**
```{r}
hourly_transfers <- project %>%
  mutate(commute_period = if_else(commute_type %in% c("Morning Commute", "Evening Commute"), "Commute","Non-Commute")) %>%
  group_by(timestamp, day_type, time_of_day, commute_period) %>%
  summarize(total_transfers = sum(transfers, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

hourly_transfers
```

Commute vs. Non-commute time periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Commute"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Non-Commute"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

Non-commute transfers have a more normal distribution than transfers during commuting hours, but both time periods have extreme values. 

Weekday vs. Weekend periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekday"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekend"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekend"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

Both distributions of transfers during the weekend and weekday are not normal, as evidenced by the extreme values and limited adherence to the Q-Q plot line.

Assumptions for T-Tests: For the t-tests evaluating commuting time periods and weekend vs. weekday transfer amounts, we assumed the sample size was large enough to be robust against normality violations. Additionally, the population standard deviation is unknown, ruling out the z-test. While the independent observation assumption may be violated due to time data, the t-test is preferred for this class.
  
```{r}
# t-test for commute time vs. non-commute time means
commute_period_test <- t.test(total_transfers ~ commute_period, data = hourly_transfers)
commute_period_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly transfers of commute periods = Mean hourly transfers of non-commute periods

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly transfers of commute periods ≠ Mean hourly transfers of non-commute periods

Because $\alpha$ = 0.05 > P-value = 1e-08, we can reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly transfer amounts during commute periods are different from the mean hourly transfer amounts during non-commute periods

```{r}
# t-test for weekday vs. weekend means
weekday_weekend_test <- t.test(total_transfers ~ day_type, data = hourly_transfers)
weekday_weekend_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly transfers on weekdays = Mean hourly transfers on weekends

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly transfers on weekdays ≠ Mean hourly transfers on weekends

Since $\alpha$ = 0.05 > P-value = 4e-06, we can reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is different from the mean hourly ridership on weekends

# Conclusions

**Key Takeaways**

Based on the EDA and analysis that was performed on this dataset, we were able to make some conclusions regarding subway ridership in New York City during the week of September 15-21, 2024. We found that many factors can influence the demand of subway ridership, such as time of day, type of day (weekdays vs. weekends), and borough. Specifically, we found that ridership varies throughout the day with commute versus non-commute periods. This is consistent with the expected commuting behavior that we hypothesized before running the analysis. We were also able to see that ridership varies by borough. Lastly, we were able to conclude that a lot of the transfer activity is concentrated in Queens, which makes sense because of the population that commutes into the city to work from Long Island.

**Limitations**

Even though we were able to draw conclusions after analyzing our data, it is important to note that there are some limitations to the analysis. First, many of the hypothesis test assumptions were not strongly satisfied at times. There may be better statistical tests to run on our data, but we stayed with t-tests and ANOVA tests because they are the tools that we know. Additionally, it is unclear if potential construction and/or closures in the subway system affected our data for the chosen week. This is not something that we were able to explore in the data, but it is a possibility that there could have been some effects from this. The data also only captures riders that pay at the turnstile when coming into the station, so ridership for individuals who do not pay was not able to be captured. Lastly, the findings from our analysis are the most generalizable to the specific week of September 15-21, 2024. Further analysis could be done during a range of different or longer time periods to consider results that may be more generalizable.
